head:
Children · Motor skills

What childhood no longer develops: strength, coordination, flexibility

A child who runs, jumps, climbs, throws and hangs from bars is building strength, balance and coordination without knowing it. Across nearly 11 million children tested in 29 countries, the standing broad jump has been declining since 2000. But the full picture is less simple than "children are weaker": some abilities are declining, others are improving, and others have not been measured. This article follows one question, from the broadest view to the most precise, up to what we can conclude and do.

The problem

When people talk about children's fitness, they almost always talk about their breathing: they run for less time, they get out of breath faster. That is measured and documented. Far less is said about what happens in the legs, the arms, the hands and the balance: the ability to jump far, to pull oneself up, to catch a ball, to stand on one foot, to bend without pain.

These abilities are built through the repetition of simple movements: climbing, jumping over an obstacle, throwing, catching, pulling, carrying. For a long time, free play supplied these repetitions without anyone having to organise them. If that play has changed form, what is left of this work? And if something is missing, does it matter for what comes next, or does a teenager catch up on everything very quickly?

The second part is the most important. People talk about developmental "windows": ages at which one would learn better. The idea is widespread in youth sport and partly disputed by researchers. We will look at what holds up.

The question

Do today's children develop less strength, coordination and flexibility than before, are there periods when this shortfall costs more, and is it paid for later in physical activity and health?

We proceed in six steps, from the general to the precise: the whole population, the comparison of abilities with one another, coordination and flexibility, developmental windows, the link with the future, then the objections. The answer comes after, with what can be done.

What is at stake

The first issue is the skeleton. During childhood and adolescence, a large share of bone is laid down, and the child's skeleton responds to impacts and loads: jumping, running, landing on one's own weight. One review links the peak bone mass reached in youth to the risk of fracture much later.10 We will see what the measurements allow us to state.

The second issue is adult health. A very large Swedish study linked muscular strength measured at 18 to the risk of death in the following decades. We will come back to it: it does not prove that adolescent strength causes lifespan, but it shows that this simple measure, taken at an age when no one thinks about it, says a lot.15

The third issue is the habit of being active. A child who is at ease in their movements likes to do them. A clumsy child risks being left on the sidelines. A model proposed in 2008 by Stodden assumes that skill, activity, fitness and weight influence one another, with links that strengthen over time. The evidence is still partial.13,17

There is also self-confidence, injury prevention, and the possibility of playing a sport in adolescence without starting from zero. And there is a decision at stake: if some abilities are declining, where should the limited time available be put? If the diagnosis is wrong, we invest in the wrong place. Hence the importance of distinguishing what is measured, what is assumed and what is false.

Step 1 of 6 · The whole population

Worldwide, children jump less far than in 2000

We start with the largest database available on a power test: the standing broad jump, with feet together and no run-up. The test is simple and needs no equipment: the child bends, swings the arms and jumps as far as possible. It relies mainly on the explosive strength of the legs, and probably on arm and leg coordination (this is reasoning, not a measurement). It does not require endurance.

A team led by Tomkinson pooled 34 studies and national datasets, covering 10,940,801 children and adolescents aged 9 to 17 in 29 countries, from 1960 to 2017.1 Over the whole period, the result is almost nil: +1.73 cm per decade, or +0.99%. That is what the average shows. But the curve has a shape: a steady rise from the 1960s to the 1980s, a slowdown in the 1990s, then a decline from 2000.1

The broad jump improved until 2000 and has declined since

Raw percentage changes, 10,940,801 children aged 9 to 17, 29 countries. The "adjusted" values (dashed) are the published estimates after accounting for children's earlier maturation. Source: Tomkinson et al., Sports Medicine, 2020.1

What this means

Between 2000 and 2017, the jump fell by 5.6% in boys and by 5.8% in girls. On a jump of 1.50 m, 5.6% represents about 8 cm (illustrative calculation). This is not a collapse, but it is a change of direction after forty years of progress, and it is of the same order in both sexes. The authors write that the decline is "suggestive" of a drop in explosive leg strength. They also note that increasingly early maturation inflated the gains before 2000, and that the real decline after 2000 is probably larger than the raw decline, around 7%.1

Of the 29 countries, 18 (62%) show a decline, mostly after 2000. The most marked is Greece, with −13.0 cm per decade from 1990 to 2014; Singapore, in the 1980s, went in the other direction.1 The global trend exists, but it is not uniform. On at least one basic ability, today's children therefore do worse than those of 2000. It remains to be seen whether this is specific to jumping or whether all abilities follow.

Step 2 of 6 · Comparing abilities with one another

Beyond cardio, abilities do not move in the same direction

To compare, we need studies that measure several abilities over the same periods. Fühner and colleagues reviewed 22 studies from 17 countries, covering 96,522 children aged 6 to 18, between 1972 and 2015, across four families of tests: cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular power (jumps), relative muscular strength (pull-ups, sit-ups) and speed.2 Endurance increased until 1986, then fell until around 2010-2012, by about 1.5 standard deviations, the largest change of the four. The other abilities moved three times less: power follows a slightly negative curve, relative strength a small overall increase, and speed a small to medium increase since 2002.2

Cardio moved the most, the other abilities much less

Approximate size of the change over 1972-2015, in standard deviations. The authors give 0.5 standard deviation in their results and "0.5 to 1.0" in their discussion for the three abilities other than cardio: the bars are therefore approximate. Source: Fühner et al., Sports Medicine, 2021.2

What this means

The most massive decline is in breathing, not in the muscles. The study does not say, however, that the muscles are fine: it takes averages from studies of uneven quality, mostly European, and measures neither coordination nor flexibility.2

"Strength" is not one single thing

We now look at three strength tests, each followed across several million children. The standing broad jump (explosive leg strength) gained 0.99% per decade. Sit-ups (trunk muscular endurance, 9,939,289 children, 31 countries, 1964-2017) gained 7.1% per decade, or 38.4% in total, but progress slowed until 2000, stopped until 2010, then reversed.1,5 Grip strength (dynamometer, 2,216,320 children, 19 countries, 1967-2017) tells the opposite story: +19.4% in total, or 3.8% per decade, with a faster rise after 2000 than before (values close to twice those of the 1960s-70s), larger in 9-12 year olds than in 13-17 year olds, and similar in girls and boys.3

Three strength tests, three different trajectories

Averages over the full period of each study, with different tests and years: we compare trends, not levels. Sources: Tomkinson et al., 2020 (jump); Dooley et al., 2020 (grip); study of sit-ups 1964-2017 (article record).1,3,5

What this means

Depending on the test, "children's strength" rises, stagnates or declines. Absolute grip strength is increasing, probably in part because children are taller and mature earlier. The authors of the study, interviewed in their university's press, say they do not know exactly why, and also mention a greater recognition of muscular strength in physical activity guidelines.4 Conversely, explosive leg strength and trunk muscular endurance, two abilities that require moving one's own weight, are the ones that are declining.

A local study sheds light on the difference. In Chelmsford (England), 10-year-old children were tested in 1998 (310), 2008 (304) and 2014 (306), with strength values adjusted for height and weight. Those of 2014 are taller and heavier, but their body mass index does not differ. Their strength is lower than in 1998 in both sexes, in grip, sit-ups and flexed-arm hang, and the decline is accelerating: from 2008 to 2014, grip loses 1.6% per year (0.6% between 1998 and 2008) and sit-ups 3.9% per year (2.6% before).6 One possible reading, not demonstrated: raw strength rises with height, strength relative to the body declines. This is a sample from a single town.

The next question is that of coordination, which none of these large studies measured.

Step 3 of 6 · Coordination and flexibility

Coordination is probably declining, flexibility remains out of reach of the data

Coordination has no natural unit. The most widely used test in children is the Körperkoordinationstest für Kinder (KTK): lateral jumps, moving platforms, one-legged hops, walking backwards on a beam. It was standardised in Germany in 1974, and its results are converted into a motor quotient whose reference average is 100.7,8 In 2015, Bardid and colleagues measured 244 Belgian and 252 Australian children aged 6 to 8. In both countries, scores are significantly lower than those of the 1974 sample: 21.3% of Belgian and 39.3% of Australian children are classed as "below average". The authors attribute the gap to less activity and more sedentary behaviour, specifying that such a study does not prove the cause.7 A more modest study, of 151 children aged 7 to 11 from a single Serbian school, finds all grades below the 1974 norm.8

On the coordination test, the children tested fall below the 1974 norm

Two separate studies, not a continuous series. Left: Bardid et al., Frontiers in Psychology, 2015. Right: Škrkar, Madić and Petrović, Facta Universitatis, 2020, total motor quotient; grade 2 is the only one in the "normal" zone (86 to 115).7,8

What this means

Two modest samples, in three countries, converge: the children tested score fewer points on the KTK than the 1974 German norm. This is a clue, not a global trend: the samples differ, decades apart, without following the same children. The chart on the left shows something else, the gap between countries: four children in ten below average in Australia versus two in ten in Belgium. The authors mention physical education, nursery school and active travel.7

And flexibility?

This is the ability on which there is the least to demonstrate. Neither Fühner, nor Tomkinson, nor Dooley track it as a trend.1,2,3 In a review of 49 studies, 4 out of 6 find a positive link between motor skills and flexibility, which the authors judge uncertain; in adolescents, a meta-analysis of 61 studies concludes that the association is "unclear".18,19 Lloyd and Oliver place the most important period between 5 and 11 years and report that boys' trunk flexibility decreases between 9 and 12 years, but recommend maintaining it rather than making it the central goal.12 The title mentions flexibility, and we must be clear: it cannot be shown that it is declining in children.

Provisional assessment: a clear decline in explosive strength, a halt then a decline in muscular endurance, coordination probably lower than in 1974, grip strength and speed that are rising, flexibility unknown. It remains to be seen why childhood would matter more than any other age.

Step 4 of 6 · Developmental windows

A solid window for bone, contested windows for the rest

The idea of a "window" says that there are ages at which an ability develops more easily. On this subject, two things must be separated: the skeleton, where there are measurements, and general motor abilities, where there are few.

For bone, the most useful study follows 2,014 American children and adolescents aged 5 to 19 for up to 7 years. At age 7, children have reached 69.5 to 74.5% of their maximum height, but only 29.6 to 38.1% of their peak bone mineral content. In the two years before and the two years after the growth peak (on average around 11-12 years in girls, 13 years in boys), they gain 32.7 to 35.8% of their maximum. 6.9 to 10.7% remains to be acquired after growth stops.9

A third of peak bone is built in four years around the growth peak

Values at the middle of the published ranges (29.6 to 38.1%; 32.7 to 35.8%; 6.9 to 10.7%). The "in between" share is a calculated remainder (100 minus the other three), and is therefore approximate. Source: McCormack et al., JAMA Pediatrics, 2017.9

What this means

At age 7, a child already has almost three quarters of their adult height but only a third of their peak bone. Bone is built mostly later, around puberty. The authors conclude that bone accumulation continues until the end of adolescence, an "underappreciated" window for optimising bone.9 An older review, citing a Canadian study, reports that at this point the most active children accumulate more bone than the least active: about 9% more in boys, 17% in girls (figures cited by the review, not re-checked in the original study).10 The McCormack study does not measure the effect of activity. The timing is measured; the effect of jumping on that timing is only reported.

For strength, speed and coordination, the windows are contested

Long-term athlete development models propose precise ages for speed, strength or coordination. Van Hooren and De Ste Croix point out that the 2005 version cites no scientific evidence, that the updates rest mostly on the idea that "what grows fast trains better", and that the 2011 work found only cross-sectional or low-quality studies. For them, "strength" or "speed" are words that are too broad (hand-eye coordination tests overlap little with one another), and progress depends on the exercise, the muscle and past experience. They recommend training all attributes at all ages. This is a critical analysis, not a systematic review, and its conclusion rests partly on reasoning.11

Lloyd and Oliver, in another model of youth physical development, say the same thing more gently: the windows of the earlier model are "largely theoretical", and most components of fitness are trainable throughout childhood. They place basic motor skills as a priority before puberty and recommend keeping them up afterwards.12

One window is therefore measured, bone. The others are debated, and no source read shows that an ability becomes impossible to develop after a certain age.

Step 5 of 6 · The link with future activity and health

Skilful children stay more active, and adolescent strength predicts the risk of death

We start with the oldest question: does a child who masters their movements become a more active adolescent? Barnett and colleagues took 481 children who took part in a school programme in 2000 and traced 276 of them in 2006-2007, in secondary school. Those who, as children, were more skilled at throwing, catching and kicking spend more time in moderate to vigorous activity (12.7% of the variation explained) and in organised activity (18.2%). Children skilled in object movements had a 10 to 20% higher chance of doing vigorous activity in adolescence.13

These figures are modest: a share of the variation, not a law. A meta-analysis of 19 studies and 15,984 participants aged 4.5 to 20.4 finds a correlation of 0.43 between motor skill and physical fitness, described as moderate to large, slightly stronger with age.14 In adolescents alone (61 studies, 22,256 adolescents), the links are smaller: 0.20 to 0.26 with activity, and −0.36 to −0.10 with weight.19 A review of 49 studies links basic movements to endurance (10 studies out of 10) and to muscular strength (12 out of 12).18 The link exists, it is moderate, it comes from observations. The authors of the 2015 review on health "trajectories" write that two questions remain open: do the links strengthen over time, and which mechanisms come first? A 2010 review of 21 articles concluded that there was a strong association with activity, and judged muscular strength and self-esteem uncertain, for lack of studies.16,17

And for health, later on?

Strength is the only one of the three subjects followed for more than twenty years. The Ortega study followed 1,142,599 Swedes, conscripts aged 16 to 19 between 1969 and 1994, for a median of 24.2 years: 26,145 deaths (2.3%). Strength was measured by knee extension, grip and elbow flexion.15

At 18, the weakest die more often in the following decades

Crude all-cause death rates, Swedish men tested at 16-19, median follow-up of 24.2 years. The percentage differences are calculated here from these rates (86.9 out of 122.3; 90.9 out of 114.5) and do not replace the study's adjusted risk ratios. Source: Ortega et al., BMJ, 2012.15

What this means

In this cohort, the weakest adolescents had a higher death rate: 122.3 versus 86.9 for the leg, 114.5 versus 90.9 for the hand. With the study's adjustments, from the fourth strength band onwards, the risk ratios are 0.78 to 0.84 compared with the weakest band; the article's abstract speaks of a 20 to 35% lower risk. The authors compare the effect with those of body mass index and blood pressure. This strength is not the one that would have been "built by playing": it is a marker measured at 18, in men, with no measure of endurance or activity, and the study cannot disentangle the causes. It finds no link with cancer.15

The chain has several links: some abilities are declining; bone has a measured window; basic movements somewhat predict future activity; strength at 18 predicts the risk of death. Each is solid on its own. The whole chain is not: no study read follows a child who plays less through to a health consequence. That is the subject of the next step.

Step 6 of 6 · Objections and what remains uncertain

What these data do not prove

First objection: different samples are being compared. The coordination decline comes from a 1974 norm, not from following generations with the same protocol. The other series rely on published averages, with varying protocols. Tomkinson and his team point out summary statistics, no individual data, no formal assessment of risk of bias, and 28 of 29 countries (97%) being high-income or upper-middle-income.1 Fühner notes large gaps between studies and the absence of maturation data.2

Second objection: children's bodies have changed. They mature earlier: first periods arrive about 0.3 years earlier each decade, which inflates the gains before 2000 and makes the decline after 2000 clearer, not smaller.1 Weight may also play a part: the authors consider that, at equal BMI, more fat mass penalises the jump. The Chelmsford study adjusts for height and weight and still finds a decline.6

Third objection: is play really what disappeared? This is the least demonstrated part of the starting hypothesis. The authors of the jump study write that there is no convincing evidence of a recent decline in overall activity; they mention the decline in cycling, jumping skills that are less practised and less confidence in one's body, and find no significant link between national jump trends and moderate to vigorous activity (correlation of 0.51, interval from −0.06 to 0.83, across few countries).1 The Chelmsford study reports lower self-reported activity in 2014 than in 2008.6 The decline is measured, its cause is not.

Fourth objection: causality may run the other way. A gifted child is more active because they succeed, and a more active child becomes more gifted. The meta-analysis on skill and fitness notes that the two types of tests may overlap.14 Genes, family environment and maturation also play a part, and the Ortega study has neither endurance nor physical activity, and covers only men.15

Fifth objection: some of the measures go the other way. Absolute grip strength is rising, speed has been rising since 2002, relative strength has a small increase. An article that showed only the declines would lie by omission, and that is why the title is more assertive than the data.

The answer to the problem

Do children develop less strength, coordination and flexibility than before? For some abilities, yes, and it is solid: explosive leg strength has declined since 2000 by 5.6 to 5.8% in raw values, probably 7% after correction for maturation, across 10.9 million children. Trunk muscular endurance, which had progressed strongly, has been stable and then declining since 2010. For coordination, it is probable but fragile: three modest samples are below the 1974 norm. For flexibility, we do not know, and absolute grip strength is rising. "Childhood no longer develops" is therefore too general: true for power and muscular endurance, plausible for coordination, not demonstrated for flexibility, false for grip.

Are there periods when it matters more? For bone, yes: a third of the maximum is built around the growth peak, and much remains to be acquired after. For the other abilities, the precise "windows" put forward by some models are not supported by direct evidence, and the two analyses read recommend working on all abilities at all ages. What is plausible, without being demonstrated: the earlier one practises, the more years of practice one has.

Is it paid for later? Probably in part, without proof of cause. A child's skill is linked to the adolescent's activity in a moderate way, and strength at 18 is linked to the risk of death. But no study read shows that a child who jumped and climbed less will pay a specific cost. What is established on another level: strength and basic movements can be measured from childhood, they can be trained, and a low result is a signal to monitor.

What to put in place

The actions are ordered. The test frequencies are an editorial choice: no study read gives any for children. The protocol and norm tables of the page's test were not provided, so the article announces no threshold.

  1. Measure with the page's test, not by eye.A jump, a grip strength measure or a balance test give a starting point. Children grow: compare with children of the same age and sex, and note the height.
  2. Give a volume of varied movements, especially before and during puberty.Jumping, climbing, throwing, catching, hanging, changing direction. For bone, Burrows' review recommends impact and loading activities, such as gymnastics or football, at least 3 sessions per week, with school programmes of 3 to 20 minutes per day.10 These are review recommendations, not an established threshold.
  3. Do not wait for a "good window" or specialise too early.The two analyses read recommend working on all abilities at all ages.11,12
  4. Work on coordination for its own sake.Balance, ball games. One study read links object skills in childhood to activity in adolescence, which justifies not limiting oneself to strength.13
  5. Retest two to three times a year, under the same conditions.Same surface, same time of day, same warm-up. A growing child jumps further without having changed anything: only a difference relative to children of the same age says something about training.

Marked clumsiness, pain on exertion or a clear delay compared with children of the same age justify talking to a paediatrician or a sports doctor.

What these figures do not say
  • The large series come mostly from high-income countries, from published averages, with no assessment of risk of bias.1,2
  • Coordination rests on two comparisons with a 1974 norm; no flexibility trend was read.7,8
  • The cause of the decline in the jump is not established, and the link with mortality comes from Swedish men tested at 18.1,15

Frequently asked questions

My child jumps less far than I thought: is that worrying?

A single result says little: tests vary from one day to the next and children grow at different rates. The studies describe averages, not diagnoses. Compare with children of the same age and sex, and retest.

Is strength training dangerous for a child?

According to Lloyd and Oliver, children can train strength safely under qualified supervision.12 This is the opinion of two authors, not a trial we have read.

Is there an age limit for learning to jump, throw or catch?

No source read shows one. The exception is bone, where the timing is measured.9,11

Are screens responsible?

No source read measures it.
